passage:
Monday. Bhupen stood at the foot of the slide ladder with four other children ahead of him. He hopped from foot to foot and tried to squeeze past a girl in a yellow frock. His aunt called, “Bhupen, look, everyone is waiting for a turn.” Lokesh, a boy in a red cap, stayed at the back and said nothing, hugging his knees.
Thursday. Bhupen counted the children in front out loud, “One, two, three,” and folded his arms.
Saturday. He waited through all five. His aunt clapped softly, and Bhupen whispered, “Now it’s my turn.” Lokesh, behind him, grinned.

qa.q: How many children were ahead of Bhupen in the queue on Monday?
qa.a: Four other children were ahead of him at the foot of the slide ladder.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling as he hopped from foot to foot on Monday?
qa.a: He felt impatient. Hopping and trying to squeeze past the girl in the yellow frock show that he wanted his turn right away.

qa.q: What small step helped Bhupen hold on while waiting on Thursday?
qa.a: Counting the children in front out loud gave him something to do with his impatience, and it made the wait feel shorter. 🙂

qa.q: What might Lokesh have been feeling, staying silent at the back on Monday?
qa.a: Lokesh may have felt uneasy watching Bhupen try to push ahead, or he may simply have been patient. His silence and hugged knees do not show for sure which.

grounding: Shows a young child slowly learning to wait for a slide turn, helped by an adult's words, counting and praise.

passage:
The bakery was hot and loud, and the line reached the door. Yusuf, five, held Papa’s hand and stared at the buns. “Why is that lady going first?” he whispered. “She came first,” said Papa. “We wait.”
Behind them a boy named Varun kept tugging his mother’s sleeve and groaning. The people in front only sighed. Yusuf’s lip wobbled. He pressed his face into Papa’s leg and counted the fan blades going round.
When the man at the counter finally nodded at them, Papa crouched down. “You waited so well.” Yusuf held out the coins.

qa.q: Who was standing behind Yusuf in the bakery line?
qa.a: A boy named Varun was behind Yusuf, tugging his mother’s sleeve and groaning.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf's lip wobble in the line?
qa.a: Yusuf was finding the wait hard. The heat, the noise and seeing the lady go first made him want to give up, so he hid his face in Papa's leg.

qa.q: How did counting the fan blades help Yusuf?
qa.a: It gave Yusuf something to do while he waited, so the impatience was easier to hold, and Papa's praise at the end told him the effort was noticed.

qa.q: How might Varun's mother feel while Varun tugs at her sleeve in the crowded line?
qa.a: She may feel tired and a little embarrassed, hoping the line moves quickly. The passage only shows the tugging and groaning, so her exact feeling is a guess.

grounding: Shows a young child waiting at a crowded counter, holding on through impatience with Papa's clear rule and praise.

passage: Teacher's note, Tuesday. At outdoor time, Parul wanted the slide straight away and tried to climb up the front. I reminded her, 'The line starts here. You're after Sunaina.' She stamped her foot and hopped from side to side, counting the children out loud. I told her, 'You're waiting so well. One more turn.' When Sunaina went down, Parul shrieked with joy and zoomed after her. Tomorrow I will put turn cards at the slide so the order is easy to see.

qa.q: Who was Parul waiting after?
qa.a: Sunaina.

qa.q: What does Parul hopping from side to side suggest?
qa.a: She felt impatient and restless, finding it hard to wait for her turn.

qa.q: What is the teacher planning, and why might it help?
qa.a: Putting turn cards at the slide so the order is easy to see, which makes waiting feel clear and fair.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel when Parul tried to climb up the front?
qa.a: Sunaina may have felt worried or cross that her turn would be taken, and relieved when the teacher kept the order.

grounding: A young child finds waiting for the slide hard and holds on with adult praise and a clear, fair order.

passage: At the village ration shop in Punjab, the line stretched past the neem tree. Rukmini held Nani's hand and hopped. 'Why can't we go first?' she whined. 'Because Jeeto aunty came first,' Nani said. Rukmini pulled at Nani's dupatta and groaned loudly. Amandeep, the shopkeeper, called out, 'Who's the best waiter in this line?' Rukmini stood very still. When their turn came, he gave her a small paper cone of roasted chana. 'For waiting,' he said. Rukmini grinned all the way home.

qa.q: Where did the line stretch to?
qa.a: Past the neem tree.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she groaned and pulled Nani's dupatta?
qa.a: She felt impatient and cross, wanting to go first.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep's question work?
qa.a: It turned waiting into something to be praised, so Rukmini tried hard to stand still.

qa.q: What might Nani feel when Rukmini grins all the way home?
qa.a: Nani is probably relieved and pleased that the waiting ended happily.

grounding: A young child learns to wait her turn in a village shop line, helped by fairness and an adult's praise.

passage: At the ice-cream van in a Madrid park, six children stood in line. Hiroshi was fifth. He bounced on his toes, then tried to slide in beside the girl at the front. 'Hey, the line!' said Javier, who was sixth. Hiroshi's mother touched his shoulder. 'Everyone's waiting, cariño. Count with me.' They counted the children getting cones: one, two, three. 'Good waiting,' she whispered. When Hiroshi finally got his strawberry cone, he turned round and let Javier pick a sprinkle colour first.

qa.q: What place was Hiroshi in the line?
qa.a: Fifth.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi try to slide in at the front?
qa.a: He felt impatient and excited, finding it hard to wait for the ice cream.

qa.q: How did Hiroshi's mother help him wait?
qa.a: She reminded him everyone was waiting, counted the cones with him and praised his good waiting.

qa.q: How might Javier feel when Hiroshi tried to slide in?
qa.a: Javier probably felt it was unfair, waiting right behind, which is why he spoke up about the line.

grounding: A young child finds waiting in line hard and manages it with a parent's calm help, counting and praise.

passage: In the playschool garden, five children lined up for the red slide. Ganga was third. She hopped from foot to foot. "Me now! Me now!" Pallavi Miss knelt beside her. "You're waiting so nicely. First Lina, then Babu, then you." Ganga held up her fingers and counted: one, two. Lina slid down. Babu slid down. Ganga's turn! At the bottom she ran straight to Miss. "I waited!" Miss gave her a high five. Then Ganga ran to the back of the line again, all by herself.

qa.q: Where was Ganga in the line for the red slide?
qa.a: Ganga was third.

qa.q: How was Ganga feeling while she hopped from foot to foot?
qa.a: She felt impatient and excited, wanting her turn right away.

qa.q: How did Pallavi Miss help Ganga keep waiting?
qa.a: She praised Ganga's waiting and said clearly who came first, so Ganga could count the turns on her fingers.

qa.q: What might Lina and Babu feel when Ganga waits instead of pushing?
qa.a: They likely feel it is fair and safe to take their turns without being pushed.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to wait for a turn at the slide, held steady by a teacher's praise and a clear order.
